# Deriving Novel Quaternary Ammonium Compound Disinfectant Scaffolds from a Natural Product: Mechanistic Insights of the Quaternization of Ianthelliformisamine C

**Authors:** Ryan A. Allen; Caroline E. M. McCormack; William M. Wuest

**Affiliations:** [a]Department of Chemistry, Emory University, 30322 Atlanta, GA (USA)

## Abstract

In the search for novel quaternary ammonium compound (QAC) disinfectants that can evade bacterial resistance, we turned to natural products as a source of inspiration. Herein we used natural product ianthelliformisamine C as a scaffold to design a small library of QACs. We first synthesized ianthelliformisamine C via an amide coupling that allowed for facile purification without the need for protecting groups. We then alkylated and quaternized the internal amines to yield four novel QACs, but all but one demonstrated no antibacterial activity against the tested strains. Using a combination of membrane depolarization and permeabilization assays, we were able to demonstrate that ianthelliformisamine C and the active QAC analog enact cell death via membrane permeabilization, contrary to prior reports on ianthelliformisamine C’s mechanism of action.

## Abstract

In the search for polypharmacological quaternary ammonium compound disinfectants, we sought to investigate the quaternization of the ianthelliformisamine C scaffold. We synthesized a small library of quaternary ammonium compounds, finding that the tetramethyl derivative had the best activity. We investigated the mechanism of action of the natural product and methylated derivative, finding that both permeabilized the membrane.

## Introduction

Quaternary ammonium compounds (QACs) are a class of antimicrobials used extensively in household and hospital antiseptic products, including disinfectant sprays and wipes, mouthwash, and antibacterial hand soap.[1] QACs are salts containing at least one quaternary nitrogen and a long alkyl chain. The structures of QACs encode their mechanism of action; the positively charged nitrogen is first electrostatically attracted to the mostly negative cell membrane of bacteria. The long alkyl chain can then intercalate into the hydrophobic phospholipid membrane, causing permeabilization. This, at high enough concentrations, can lead to pore formation and loss of intracellular contents, all leading to cell lysis and death.[2–6]

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused a major increase in the use of QAC-based disinfectants as schools, businesses, healthcare facilities, and households implemented more frequent cleaning procedures to slow the transmission of SARS-CoV-2.[7,8] In fact, 303 the 654 disinfectants listed on the Environmental Protection Agency’s List N: Disinfectants for Coronavirus (COVID-19), which designates products approved by the EPA to effectively kill SARS-CoV-2, contain QACs as an active ingredient.[9] The increased quantities of QACs used during the pandemic may have unintended consequences, as QACs persist and accumulate in the environment. For example, the photocatalyzed half-life of benzalkonium chloride in surface waters is 12–94 days.[10] More worrisome than this extended half-life in light accessible water is the concentration in bay sediments, as it has been shown that QACs persist in these regions due to their adsorption to the clay lattices.[11] An increase in environmental and biological concentrations of QACs during the pandemic has been documented, as two recent studies have detected greater concentrations of QACs in household dust and human blood samples compared to before 2020.[12,13]

This accumulation of QACs in the environment is concerning because bacteria can develop resistance after prolonged exposure to sub-inhibitory concentrations of QACs.[1] One nuanced mechanism of resistance is membrane rigidification, which has been seen in the increased concentration of saturated fatty lipids and decreased concentration of unsaturated fatty lipids in Acinetobacter baumannii membranes after prolonged exposure to sub-minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of benzalkonium chloride (BAC).[14] This was recapitulated in Pseudomonas putida.[15] However, the most common mechanism of resistance to QACs is efflux pumps, such as QacA and QacB, that can confer resistance to antibiotics as well as QACs.[16–18] Additionally, conjugative plasmids containing such efflux pumps found in Staphylococcus aureus are known to often carry resistance genes to other antibiotics such as dfrA, causing trimethoprim resistance, and aacA-aphD, causing gentamycin and kanamycin resistance.[19–22] These plasmids, specifically pSK1, are widespread in S. aureus clinical isolates, and are hypothesized to not come at a significant fitness cost to the cell.[20] As such, combatting QAC resistance is a necessary part of the broader fight against antibiotic resistant bacteria, which are responsible for 2.8 million infections and 35,000 deaths in the United States annually.[23]

Developing novel QACs is a crucial step in responding to antimicrobial resistance. One potential source of novel QAC scaffolds is natural products because of their structural and functional diversity.[24,25 Particularly, developing QACs from the structures of antimicrobial natural products may lead to novel antimicrobials with a higher barrier to the development of resistance. If the novel QAC retains the mechanism of action (MoA) of the original antimicrobial and obtains the membrane permeabilization functionality of a QAC, this could create a polypharmacological disinfectant. Polypharmacological antimicrobials, which display multiple intrinsic MoAs, often have a higher barrier to the development of resistance because bacteria have to acquire multiple adaptations to develop resistance.[26–28] This is epitomized by tyrothricin, a combination of cyclic peptides, that has been in clinical use for over 7 decades but has not had clinical resistance development.[29] This has been attributed to the polypharmacological MoA of one component tyrocidine A, which not only rigidifies and permeabilizes the membrane, but also interferes with DNA binding proteins and causes DNA damage.[30] The synthesis of antimicrobial natural product-based QACs has been demonstrated by Okano and coworkers, who appended QAC moieties to the antibiotic vancomycin, resulting in increased potency.[31,32] Additionally, when polymyxin B was appended with quaternary ammoniums by Ongwae and coworkers, the best analogs retained similar potency to the natural product as well as switched from narrow spectrum, gram-negative activity to broad spectrum activity.

In order to develop QACs with polypharmacological properties, we focused on the quaternization of ianthelliformisamine C (1, (Figure 1)). This natural product, originally isolated from a sea sponge, was found to have strong activity against both Pseudomonas aeruginosa and S. aureus, with MICs of 17.5 μM and 8.75 μM, respectively.[33] Its total synthesis was first published by Pieri and coworkers, who reported that an analog similar in structure to ianthelliformisamine C enacted its MoA via depolarization of the membrane.[34] Ianthelliformisamine C has also been found to have inhibitory activity against both human and Mycobacterium tuberculosis carbonic anhydrases, thereby giving it a polypharmacological MoA.[35,36] In addition to ianthelliformisamine C, a similarly structured natural product QAC pulmonarin B was found to have cholinesterase inhibitory activity (Figure 1).[37] When compared to P. aeruginosa and S. aureus genomes in a protein BLAST search, homologous proteins for both human and M. tuberculosis carbonic anhydrases as well as human cholinesterase were found in both species (Table 1).[38–40] Therefore, we hypothesize that ianthelliformisamine C is inhibiting P. aeruginosa and S. aureus in a polypharmacological manner. We thus proceeded with the total synthesis of ianthelliformisamine C and its quaternary ammonium derivatives, hypothesizing we could develop polypharmacological disinfectants.

## Results and Discussion

### Total Synthesis of Ianthelliformisamine C and QAC Analogs

The total synthesis of ianthelliformisamine C started with a Wittig reaction utilizing 3,5-dibromo-4-hydroxybenzaldehyde to give the conjugated E-alkene product 3, following the synthesis developed by Pieri and coworkers (Scheme 1).[34] After methylation and hydrolysis to give acid 5, the conditions originally reported by Pieri and coworkers that leveraged a one-step DCC coupling to synthesize 1 in 70% yield was attempted; however, we were unable to replicate the yield due to the arduous purification required to separate the multiple byproducts, unreacted intermediates, and starting materials from the desired product.

We therefore screened a number of different coupling conditions as well as direct amidations from the ester (Table S1). The optimal conditions leveraged the activated N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS) ester 6, followed by amidation with spermine to yield 1 in 69% yield. The QAC analogs were then simply made by first subjecting 1 to a reductive amination with either formaldehyde or long alkyl aldehydes to yield N-alkylated 7–10 in good to moderate yields (Scheme 1). Treatment of these molecules with methyl iodide gave the desired QACs 11–14 in moderate to poor yields due to the required trituration with hot ethyl acetate as purification. These molecules were moved forward for biological testing.

### Biological Investigations of Ianthelliformisamine C and QAC Analogs

To assess the antibacterial activity of the synthesized natural product and QAC analogs, MIC assays were conducted (Table 2). Ianthelliformisamine C (1) had the best activity out of all the analogs tested, and this work expanded upon the strains tested against this natural product. Its activity against P. aeruginosa was on par with the values reported in the original isolation report by Xu and coworkers.[33] The activity was 4-fold worse against PA14 compared to PAO1, likely due to PA14 being hypervirulent, which can cause antibiotic resistance via upregulation of efflux pumps and biofilm formation.[41,42]

Additionally, this work demonstrates the potency of this natural product against both community-acquired (CA) and hospital-acquired (HA) methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), which has not been previously reported. Interestingly, the methylation of the free amines (7) drastically reduces the activity of the natural product against all bacteria tested. We hypothesized that the dimethylation either disrupts protein binding or makes the molecule a worse protonophore. The long chain QACs had no antibacterial activity, likely due to their hydrophobicity and inability to dissolve in the testing solution. However, the tetramethyl QAC 11 was active and had moderate to good activity against all strains tested. Additionally, this QAC had a low human toxicity as measured by hemolysis20 (Lysis20, Table 2), or the concentration at which 20% of red blood cells are lysed. This lysis value gives this QAC a better therapeutic index than commercial benzalkonium chloride (1 to 15.6 versus 0.5 to 8, respectively). Additionally, it had reduced efficacy against HA-MRSA, which has been reported to be more antibiotic resistant.[43]

To further investigate the MoA of the natural product and QAC derivative in gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, we utilized depolarization and permeabilization assays against S. aureus and P. aeruginosa. To detect depolarization of the cell, we used the voltage sensitive dye 3,3’-dipropylthiadicarbocyanine iodide (DiSC3(5)), as previously reported.[34,44] As a positive control, we used benzalkonium chloride (BAC), which is known to permeabilize membranes and thus destroy the proton gradient.2 In line with a previous report by Pieri and coworkers that used an analog of ianthelliformisamine C (15, Figure 3), 1 was found to depolarize S. aureus in a dose dependent manner (Figure 2A).[34] Interestingly, the N.N’-dimethyl analog 7 was found to depolarize the cell to a statistically significantly higher extent than 1. This was unexpected because 7 had lower activity than 1 in the MIC assays. This indicates that N,N’-dimethylation does not impact the core structure’s ability to disrupt the proton gradient, but could disrupt protein binding. To differentiate between depolarization and permeabilization, we used propidium iodide DNA staining to detect pore formation and permeabilization of the cell.[45] To our surprise, we found that 1 permeabilizes the cell at concentrations above the MIC (Figure 2B), which contradicts the previous report on the analog 15 (Figure 3). This implies that the analog has a different MoA than 1, likely due to their quite different structures, and is therefore not an accurate proxy for the natural product.[34] Additionally, 7 was found to not induce permeabilization of the cell, indicating that the differences in their activities could be due to nuances in membrane disruption. QAC analog 11 was found to both depolarize and permeabilize the cell, in line with the typical MoA of QACs. The time course data for S. aureus membrane depolarization can be found in Figure S1 A-D and the membrane permeabilization time course data can be found in Figure S2 A-D.

For the gram-negative P. aeruginosa, we started with permeabilization assays as we saw significant permeabilization of the gram-positive S. aureus and permeabilization necessitates depolarization. We first conducted a nitrocefin hydrolysis assay to assess outer membrane integrity (Figure 2C, Figure 4). Nitrocefin is cleaved in the presence of β-lactamases that can only be accessed when the outer membrane is permeabilized.[34,46] Using polymyxin B (PMB) as a positive control, we discovered that 1 and 11 both permeabilized the outer membrane at 0.5 times their respective MICs, and they did so in a dose-dependent manner. 11 was also found to permeabilize the outer membrane to a statistically significant higher extent than BAC. This permeabilization can be visualized in both the bar graph endpoint absorbances after one hour and in the time course data of each compound at 2x their respective MICs. The time course data for each compound at each concentration is shown in Figure S3 A–D. To interrogate inner membrane stability, we again employed propidium iodide to detect DNA staining via pore formation (Figure 2D).[47,48] We observed dose dependent permeabilization of the inner membrane, thereby confirming that natural product 1 and QAC analog 11 are acting as membrane permeabilizers and not protonophores. Additionally, BAC permeabilized the inner membrane to a statistically significantly higher amount than 11, suggesting that the differences in permeabilization of each membrane likely arises from the differences in affinity of each molecule to the inner and outer membranes. The time course data for inner membrane permeabilization can be found in Figure S4 A–D.

## Conclusions

To investigate the potential to develop polypharmacological quaternary ammonium compounds, we undertook the total synthesis of ianthelliformisamine C for development into novel QAC structures. We leveraged a two-step amide coupling to allow for uncomplicated purifications and a 36% overall yield in five steps. We then synthesized a small library of QAC analogs and confirmed only the tetramethyl QAC 11 had activity against the tested strains, likely because the long chain QACs were insoluble in the testing media. We demonstrated that the N,N’-dimethylated natural product 7 had diminished activity against all strains tested, and determined that this decrease was not due to a decrease in the core scaffold’s protonophore activity, but possibly due to its lack of membrane permeabilization. We also demonstrated that the natural product 1, in addition to potential protein inhibition, is also enacting its mechanism of action via permeabilization of bacterial membranes and not depolarization as previously hypothesized. We also found that the tetramethyl QAC analog 11 had moderate to good activity against all strains tested and had diminished human toxicity as measured by hemolysis. Additionally, we found that 11 inhibits bacterial growth via permeabilization of the cell membranes, much like commercial QAC benzalkonium chloride.
